docs.text: This block diagram shows the basic overview of my subsystem. Important things to mention are the power supply, connection to teammates and the IR sensor. The IR matched pair and the Op-amp have two options due to the need for refinement from testing. Both have the same power draw and can in theory produce needed output.

docs.title: Component Selection
docs.text:
Input Op amp

  1. CA3140AEZ MOSFET‑input op amp

    • $3.78/each
    • link to product
    Pros Cons Very high input impedance ideal for weak heart‑rate sensor signals Not rail‑to‑rail limits output swing in low voltage designs Wide supply range (4 V–36 V) Older design with limited availability Low offset voltage stable baseline for pulse detection Requires external biasing and filtering

  • ~$0.60/each
  • Link to product
Pros Cons Rail-to-rail input and output maximizes signal range on 3.3 V and 5 V systems Lower bandwidth (1 MHz) than many high-speed op-amps Very low power consumption (100 µA typical per amplifier) Not ideal for high-frequency or RF applications Includes four op-amps in one package, reducing PCB space and cost Moderate input offset voltage (4.5 mV typical) Operates from 1.8 V to 6 V, making it ideal for battery-powered sensor circuits Limited slew rate (0.6 V/µs) for fast-changing signals Extremely low input bias current (1 pA typical) works well with photodiodes and sensor interfaces

  1. TL081CP JFET‑input op amp

    • $0.65/each
    • link to product
    Pros Cons JFET‑input like CA3140 excellent for high impedance heart‑rate sensors Requires dual supply for full performance in some configurations High slew rate (13 V/µs) preserves pulse waveform shape Not rail to rail reduced output swing at low voltages Through‑hole DIP‑8 easy prototyping and breadboard‑friendly Slightly higher input bias current than CA3140

docs.title: MCP6004-I/P Low-Power Quad Rail-to-Rail Op Amp
Why the MCP6004 is the best op‑amp choice
docs.text:
The MCP6004 is a good op amp because it is low-power, rail-to-rail, and works with 3.3 V or 5 V supplies. It also includes four op amps in one chip, making it a compact and cost-effective choice for sensor and microcontroller projects like a heart rate monitor.

IR TX and RX Pair

  1. TSAL6200 (IR Transmitter) + TSOP38238 (IR Receiver)

    • TX: $0.72/each — TSAL6200
    • RX: $1.18/each — TSOP38238
    • link to TX
    • link to RX
    Pros Cons Very strong IR output excellent for reflective heart‑rate sensing Requires 38 kHz modulation for proper RX operation Through‑hole easy to mount and prototype RX has narrow detection bandwidth High sensitivity receiver reduces noise in pulse detection TX requires current‑limiting resistor

  2. SFH4550 (IR Transmitter) + SFH213 (IR Photodiode)

    • TX: $0.48/each — SFH4550
    • RX: $0.62/each — SFH213
    • link to TX
    • link to RX
    Pros Cons Photodiode RX allows analog signal extraction ideal for heart‑rate waveform Requires external amplifier (op‑amp stage) Wide‑angle IR LED improves skin illumination More sensitive to ambient light than demodulated receivers Very inexpensive pair Requires careful PCB layout for noise reduction

  3. LTE‑4208 (IR LED) + LTR‑4206E (IR Phototransistor)

    * TX: $0.38/each — LTE‑4208 * RX: $0.52/each — LTR‑4206E * link to TX * link to RX

    Pros Cons Matched LED + phototransistor pair ideal for reflective heart‑rate sensing Phototransistor slower response than photodiode Through‑hole DIP package easy to mount and prototype More sensitive to ambient IR interference Good sensitivity for low cost PPG setups Requires external biasing and filtering circuitry

docs.title: Why the SFH4550 + SFH213 pair is the best IR choice
docs.text: The SFH4550 + SFH213 pair is ideal for a DIY heart rate sensor because it gives you a true analog photoplethysmography signal rather than a digital IR presence output. The SFH4550’s wide angle IR emission illuminates the skin evenly while the SFH213 photodiode produces a fast, linear current response that captures subtle blood‑volume changes accurately. Both parts are through hole, easy to mount on a custom PCB, and work perfectly with a transimpedance amplifier like the CA3140. This combination yields a clean, responsive waveform that can be filtered and amplified without fighting the limitations of slower phototransistors or demodulated IR receivers.
